Authority, Abode of life, Maker of life, Life of life, Reality, Knower of reality, One Self, Beyond birth, death and old age.
Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven-tree, Saviour, Savita, Great-grandfather, Sacrifice, Lord of sacrifice, Sacrificer, Limb of sacrifice, Bearer of sacrifice.
Supporter of sacrifice, Maker of sacrifice, Possessor of sacrifice, Enjoyer of sacrifice, Means of sacrifice, Ender of sacrifice, Secret of sacrifice, Food and eater of food.
Self-born, Born by himself, Vaikhana, Singer of Saman, Son of Devaki, Creator, Lord of the earth, Destroyer of sin.
Bearer of the conch, of Nandaka, of the discus, Wielder of the Sharnga bow, Bearer of the mace, Chariot-wheel in hand, Unshakable, Whose weapons are all that strike.
Thus the thousand divine names of the praiseworthy great soul Keshava have been fully proclaimed.
A man who always hears this and who recites it will meet nothing inauspicious here or hereafter.
A brahmin will go to the end of the Vedas, a kshatriya will be victorious, a vaishya rich in wealth, and a shudra will gain happiness.
Seeking dharma he gains dharma, seeking wealth he gains wealth, seeking desires he gains desires, and seeking offspring he gains offspring.
A devoted man who rises early, pure, with mind fixed on him, and recites these thousand names of Vasudeva,
wins vast fame and pre-eminence among kinsmen, gains unshakable fortune and the highest good.
He meets fear nowhere, finds vigour and splendour, becomes free of disease, radiant, and endowed with strength, beauty and virtues.
The sick is freed from disease, the bound from bonds, the fearful from fear, and one in distress from distress.
A man who praises the Supreme Person with the thousand names, always full of devotion, quickly crosses hard places.
A mortal who takes refuge in Vasudeva and is devoted to Vasudeva, purified of all sin, goes to eternal Brahman.
The devotees of Vasudeva never meet anything inauspicious; fear of birth, death, old age and disease does not arise.
One who studies this hymn with faith and devotion is joined with well-being of self, patience, glory, steadfastness, memory and fame.
Neither anger nor envy, neither greed nor evil thought arises in the devotees of the Supreme Person who have done good deeds.
Heaven with the moon, sun and stars, the sky, the directions, earth and the great ocean are upheld by the might of the great soul Vasudeva.
This whole world, with gods, asuras and gandharvas, yakshas, serpents and rakshasas, moving and unmoving, lies under Krishna's control.
The senses, mind, intellect, goodness, radiance, strength and steadfastness are said to have Vasudeva as their self, and so are the field and the knower of the field.
Conduct is first conceived as the basis of all traditions; dharma arises from conduct, and the lord of dharma is Achyuta.
Sages, ancestors, gods, great elements and constituents, and this moving and unmoving world arose from Narayana.
Yoga, knowledge, Sankhya, the sciences, the arts and action, the Vedas, the scriptures and wisdom: all this is from Janardana.
Vishnu is one great being, and beings are many and separate; pervading the three worlds, the self of beings, the imperishable enjoys the universe.
This hymn to the blessed Vishnu, recited by Vyasa, should be read by one who wishes to gain the good and happiness.
Those who worship the lotus-eyed lord of the universe, the unborn god, the origin and dissolution of the world, do not meet defeat.
[Bhishma] Disrespect to brahmins can bring down even the gods; one who salutes brahmins, Yudhishthira, is not harmed.
They are to be honoured, to be saluted, and you should treat them like sons; for those wise ones uphold all these worlds.
Brahmins are the great dharma-bridges of all the worlds, delighting in giving up wealth and devoted to restraint of speech.
Delightful to beings, a store of vows, firm in vows, leaders of the worlds and renowned in the scriptures,
whose wealth is always austerity, whose great strength is speech, the source of dharmas, knowers of dharma, subtle in sight,
desiring dharma, established in dharma, dharma-bridges by their good deeds, on whom all four kinds of creatures depend for life.
They are the paths, the leaders of all, the eternal bearers of sacrifice, always bearing the heavy yoke of father and grandfather.
Like good oxen they do not sink under the yoke on uneven ground; with ancestors, gods and guests as their first concern, they eat the offering of gods and ancestors first.
Treasuries of all the arts, skilful, subtle in sight, knowing the course of all beings, thinking on the course of the Self,
knowing beginning, middle and end, their doubts cut, knowing the higher and lower distinctions, going to the supreme goal,
freed, their sins shaken off, free of dualities and possessions, worthy of honour and ever honoured by the great souls who know knowledge.
They are equal toward sandal and filth, food and fasting; to them fine silk, hemp, linen and deer-skin are the same.
They can remain without eating for many days and dry up their bodies by study, with senses restrained.
They could make a non-god a god and a god a non-god, and, angered, create other worlds and world-guardians.
The sea cannot be drunk because of the curse of those great souls; the fire of their wrath still does not die down in Dandaka.
They are the gods of the gods, the cause of the cause, the authority of authority; what wise man would overpower them?
Among them the old and the young alike deserve honour, but they honour one another especially for austerity and learning.
An unlearned brahmin is a god, a great and purifying vessel; a learned one is even more a god, like a full ocean.
A brahmin, learned or unlearned, is a great deity, as fire, consecrated or not, is a great deity.
Even in the cremation ground the radiant fire is not defiled, and carrying the oblation in sacrifices it shines still more.
So even if a brahmin acts in unwanted ways in all his actions, he is always to be honoured; know him as supreme deity.
[Bhishma] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between the Wind and Arjuna, O Bharata.
Kartavirya, glorious, bearing a thousand arms, became lord of all this world at Mahishmati, of great might.
That Haihaya of true valour ruled the whole earth, with its jewel mines, its islands and its sea-girt expanse.
He gave his wealth to Dattatreya for a cause, putting kshatriya dharma first, with humility and learning.
The son of Kritavirya propitiated that sage and, glad, invited the brahmin to give three boons.
Asked by him to choose boons, the king said: "May I have a thousand arms in the midst of the army, and otherwise at home.
Let soldiers in battle see my thousand arms; may I conquer the whole earth by valour, O sage of great vows, and having won it by dharma, guard it tirelessly.
The fourth boon I ask of you, best of brahmins, blameless one: out of favour to me, give it. Let the good instruct me when I fall into wrong conduct."
Then, mounting his chariot, bright as fire and sun, he said in the confusion of his might: "Who is there like me in valour, steadfastness, fame, purity, prowess or vigour?"
At the end of his words a bodiless voice in the sky said: "Fool, you do not know that a brahmin is better than a kshatriya. A kshatriya protects subjects together with a brahmin."
[Arjuna] "Pleased, I could create beings; angered, I could bring destruction. In deed, mind and word there is no brahmin superior to me.
The first view has the brahmin as higher, the second the kshatriya; of the two reasons you stated, a difference is seen here.
Brahmins depend on the kshatriya; the kshatriya does not depend on a brahmin. Brahmins, dependent ones, devour kshatriyas on earth under pretext of Brahman.
Dharma rests in kshatriyas, the protection of subjects; brahmins' livelihood is from the kshatriya; how then is a brahmin better?
Those brahmins, foremost of all beings, always living by begging, esteemed by themselves, I shall bring under my control.
This maiden Gayatri has declared the truth in heaven; I shall conquer all brahmins, helpless, clad in skins.
No one in the three worlds, god or man, could drive me from my kingdom; therefore I am senior to a brahmin.
Today I shall make the world kshatriya-supreme, not Brahman-supreme; no one in battle can bear my strength."
Hearing Arjuna's words, the night-wandering voice was frightened; then the Wind, standing in the sky, spoke to him.

Give up this foul disposition and salute brahmins. If you do wrong to them, there will be unrest in your kingdom.
mahabharata:13:137.23	Or, O lord of the earth, the twice-born will calm you, or those of great might will cast you from the kingdom, your zeal destroyed.
The king said to him, "Who are you?" Then the Wind answered: "I am the Wind, a messenger of the gods, and I tell you what is good for you."
[Arjuna] "Ah, you have today shown devotion and love for brahmins. Tell me which brahmin is like the earth.
Tell me a brahmin like the wind, best of brahmins, tell me one like water, or like the sun or the sky."
Out of rivalry with King Anga, the Earth gave up her earthhood and went to ruin; the brahmin Kashyapa propped her up.
Brahmins, O king, are imperishable, in heaven and here, always. Long ago Angiras himself drank the waters by his radiance.
Drinking them like milk, the great ascetic was not satisfied, and filled the whole earth with a great flood, O king.
When he was angered I left the world and went, and I stayed long in the Agnihotra for fear of Angiras.
The blessed Purandara was cursed by Gautama for desiring Ahalya, though he was not killed, for the sake of dharma.
So the ocean, O king, though full of sweet water, was cursed by brahmins and made salty.
The golden-hued, smokeless fire with its flame gathered upward was cursed by the angry Angiras and deprived of these qualities.
See the Maruts, crushed, who laughed at the great ocean and were always cursed by the golden-bearing twice-born.
The great kingdom of Dandaka was destroyed by a brahmin, and the great kshatriya force of Talajangha by Aurva alone.
And by Dattatreya's grace you have gained vast kingdom, strength, dharma and learning, so hard to obtain.
Arjuna, why do you always sacrifice to Fire? Is he not a brahmin? Do you not know him as the carrier of oblations for the whole world?
Or why, knowing the best of brahmins, who follows and protects beings and is the maker of the living world, are you bewildered?
Likewise Prajapati Brahma, unmanifest, source and dissolution, by whom this whole universe, moving and unmoving, was produced.
Some unlearned wish Brahma to be egg-born. From the burst egg came mountains, directions, water, earth and sky.
This should not be seen so; how could he be greater? The sky is held to be the egg; the Grandsire was born from it.
Tell me how it could stand; there would then be nothing. He is called ego, the lord who has gone into all radiance.
There is no egg, but there is Brahma, O king, the creator of worlds. So addressed, he then fell silent, and the Wind spoke to him.
[Earth] "Having obtained this boon, the king who holds me, the support of all beings, how does he wish to give me to brahmins, Brahma's daughter?
I shall leave and go; being earth is Brahma's station. Let this king not be with his kingdom." And so she went.
Then Kashyapa, seeing the Earth going, entered the earth at once, releasing himself in concentration.
Stopped, she became thick with grass and herbs on all sides; the earth became supreme in dharma, her fear lost, O king.
So for thirty thousand divine years Kashyapa, of great vows, tirelessly was the earth, O king.
Then, O great king, the Earth came, bowed to Kashyapa, and became Kashyapi, the great soul's daughter.
Such, O king, was the brahmin Kashyapa. Name another, or tell me a kshatriya better than Kashyapa."
The king was silent, and the Wind spoke again: "Hear, O king, of Utathya, born in the family of Angiras.
She practised fierce austerity, fortunate and renowned; for him she chose the fortunate Utathya.
Then, summoning Utathya, he gave the renowned woman to him as wife, and he, giver of rich fees, took her by rule.
The glorious Varuna had desired her before; coming to the forest hermitage he carried her off on the Yamuna.
The lord of waters, having taken her, led her to his own city, wondrously splendid, with six hundred thousand lakes.
There is no city lovelier than that one, adorned with palaces, divine apsarases and pleasures; there the god, lord of waters, sported with her, O king.
Then the abduction of his wife was told to Utathya.
Hearing all that from Narada, Utathya said to Narada: "Go and speak harsh words to Varuna: at my word release my wife; why have you taken her?
You are the world's guardian, not a robber of the world. My wife was given by Soma, and you have carried her off today."
So addressed at his word by Narada, the lord of waters said, "Release Utathya's wife"; then Varuna said to him: "She is my dear wife; I cannot give her up."
Thus addressed by Varuna, Narada returned to that sage and said to Utathya, as if not very glad:
Seized by the neck, I was thrown out by Varuna, great sage. He will not give back your wife; do what you must.
Hearing Narada's words, Angiras flared up in anger and, steadying himself, the great ascetic drank the water by his radiance.
While all the water was being drunk, the lord of waters, though urged by friends, still did not release her.
Then the angry Utathya, best of brahmins, said to the Earth: "Show, fair one, the place of the six hundred thousand lakes."
Then that place became desert, and the ocean withdrew; and the best of the twice-born said to the river from that place:
Go unseen, timid Sarasvati, toward the desert; let this region be unholy, abandoned by you, fair one.
When that region was crushed, the lord of waters took the auspicious woman, went for refuge, and gave the wife to Angiras's son.
Having taken back his wife, Utathya was glad, and released the world from sorrow, and Varuna too, O Haihaya.
Then, having got his wife back, the very radiant Utathya, knower of dharma, said to Varuna what I now tell, O king, hear it.
I won her by my austerity as you cried out, lord of waters. Having said this, he took her and went to his own house.
Such, O king, was Utathya, bull among brahmins; I tell you, or you tell me, of a kshatriya better than Utathya."
The gods were conquered by the asuras and left without spirit; all their sacrifices were taken, and the svadha for the ancestors too.
The rites and worship of men were seized by the danavas, O bull of the Haihayas; deprived of lordship, the gods wandered the earth, so it is heard.
Then once, O king, they saw Agastya, blazing with radiance like the sun, of great vows and full of splendour.
Greeting him and seeing him wreathed in fame, the gods spoke these words to the great soul at the right time, O lord of men.
We were broken in battle by the danavas and deprived of lordship; therefore save us from this fierce fear, best of sages.
Thus addressed by the gods, Agastya grew angry, and the radiant one blazed like the fire of dissolution at the end.
By that net of blazing rays the danavas were burned and fell by thousands from the sky, O great king.
Burned by Agastya's radiance, those daityas gave up both worlds and fled to the southern quarter.
So the danavas were burned by the blessed Agastya, by his own radiance, O king, he whose soul was perfected by austerity.
Such too is Agastya, as told to you by me, blameless one. I tell you, or you tell me, of a kshatriya better than Agastya."
So addressed, he fell silent, and the Wind then said: "Hear, O king, the chief deed of the renowned Vasishtha.
The Adityas held a long sacrifice by Lake Manasa; having gone to Vasishtha in mind and heard his range there,
seeing them sacrificing, anxious and emaciated by the consecration, mountain-like danavas named Khalins wished to kill them.
Not far from there was a lake with a boon given by Brahma; the danavas killed there were revived by bathing in it.
Seizing terrible clubs, bars and trees, they rose out of the water a hundred yojanas, churning it.
Ten thousand of them rushed upon the gods; harassed by them, the gods went to Vasava for refuge.
Troubled by them, Shakra went to Vasishtha for refuge, and then the blessed sage Vasishtha gave them freedom from fear.
Knowing them distressed, the sage, devoted to compassion, burned all the Khalins without effort by his own radiance.
The great ascetic brought from Kailasa the famed river Ganga to that divine lake, and by her that lake was split.
The lake split by the river became the Sarayu, and the place where the Khalins were killed was called Khalina.
So the dwellers of heaven with Indra were protected by Vasishtha, and the daityas with Brahma's boon were slain by the great soul.
This deed of Vasishtha has been told to you by me, blameless one. I tell you, or you tell me, of a kshatriya better than Vasishtha."
In dense darkness the gods and danavas fought together; there the sun and moon were pierced by arrows.
Then, seized by darkness, the gods, O tiger among kings, were struck down together with the strong ones by the danavas.
Struck by the asuras, the dwellers of heaven, their life ebbing, saw the brahmin Atri practising austerity in a great forest.
Then the gods said to him, whose anger was calm and senses mastered: "These two, the moon and sun, are pierced by arrows of the asuras.
We too are being killed by enemies in the shrouding darkness and find no peace; from fear, protect us, lord."
How shall I protect you? he said; they said, "Be the moon, be the sun that destroys darkness and the robbers."
So addressed, Atri, pleasant to see like the moon, took on a gentle nature and the sun's appearance.
Seeing the moon and sun not very bright, O king, Atri by his own austerity made light in the battle.
See, royal sage, what Atri did, the sage alone, murmuring prayers, clad in skins, living on fruit.
The deed of the great soul Atri has been told at length. I tell you, or you tell me, of a kshatriya better than Atri."
So addressed, Arjuna fell silent, and the Wind said to him: "Hear, O king, the great deed of the great soul Chyavana.
Having promised the Ashvins, Chyavana said to Pakashasana, with the gods: 'Make the two Ashvins soma-drinkers.'
[Indra] 'How can these two become soma-drinkers when excluded by us? They are not counted with the gods; do not say so to us.
We do not wish, great one, to drink soma with the Ashvins; others may drink as they like, but I will not drink here.'
[Chyavana] 'If you do not do what I say, slayer of Bala, you will drink soma at the sacrifice, pressed out by me at once.'
Then, for the Ashvins' good, Chyavana suddenly began the rite, and by his mantras the gods were overcome.
Seeing the rite begun, Indra, struck senseless with rage, raised a huge mountain and rushed upon Chyavana with his thunderbolt, his eyes dim with fury.
Seeing him rush, the ascetic Chyavana sprinkled him with water and froze him, with thunderbolt and mountain.
Then the great sage created a very terrible enemy of Indra: Mada, made of mantra-offering, with open mouth.
It had a thousand teeth a hundred yojanas long, its fangs very terrible, two hundred yojanas long; one jaw was on the earth and one touched heaven.
All the gods with Vasava stood at the root of his tongue, come into the mouth of that Timi like fishes in the great ocean.
Then the gods, having consulted, gone into Mada's mouth, said together to Shakra, "Bow to this twice-born; we shall drink soma with the Ashvins, free of fever."
Then Shakra bowed and did that for Chyavana, and Chyavana made the two Ashvins soma-drinkers.
Then the sage withdrew his rite and divided Mada among dice, hunting, drink and women, the mighty one.
By these faults a man goes to ruin, O king, without doubt; therefore a man should always keep far from them.
This deed of Chyavana has been told to you, O king. I tell you, or you tell me, of a kshatriya better than Chyavana."
When the gods with Indra had come into Mada's mouth, then Chyavana took away their earth.
Thinking both worlds taken, the gods were grieved and, afflicted by sorrow, went to the great soul Brahma for refuge.
[The gods] "We were anointed with the mouth of Mada, world-honoured one; the earth was taken by Chyavana, and heaven by the Kapas, lord."
[Brahma] "Go quickly to brahmins for refuge, gods with Indra; having appeased them you will have both worlds as before."
They went to the brahmins for refuge, and the brahmins said, "Whom shall we conquer?" The gods said, "Conquer the Kapas here on earth, for we shall be the conquerors," O king.
Then the brahmins began a rite for destroying the Kapas; hearing it, the wealthy Kapa sent a messenger to the brahmins.
That messenger of the wealthy Kapa said to the brahmins: "All the Kapas are like you; what is the matter here?
All know the Veda, are wise, all sacrifice, all are true to vows, all are equal to great sages.
They offer to the blazing fire, stand by the word of their elders, are all self-controlled, and share with the weak.
They travel in carts, do not approach a menstruating woman, do not eat when those depending on them have not eaten, and do not eat or sleep by day.
Endowed with these and many other virtues, how will you conquer the Kapas? Turn back; it is well for you if you turn back."
[Brahma's side] "We shall conquer the Kapas; those who are gods are we, it is held. Therefore the Kapas are to be killed by us, wealthy one; go as you came."
The wealthy one went and told the Kapas, "The brahmins are not friendly to you." Then all the Kapas took weapons and rushed upon the brahmins.
Seeing all the Kapas with raised banners, the twice-born loosed blazing fires that destroy the Kapas' lives.
The eaters of oblations, made by Brahma, eternal, having devoured the Kapas, shone like clouds in the sky, O king, and the gods praised the twice-born and the renowned Brahma.
Their radiance and strength then grew for the gods, and they gained immortality and honour in the three worlds.
Having heard these words from the Wind, Arjuna replied, honouring him: "Hear, O mighty-armed one, what I say, O king.
I live always, lord, for the sake of brahmins; I always bow to Brahma and to brahmins.
By Dattatreya's grace I have gained this fame, and supreme renown in the world, and great dharma practised.
Ah, the deeds of brahmins as you, Wind, have told truly and in full, I have heard attentively."
[Wind] "Protect brahmins by kshatriya dharma, and your senses; fierce danger from the Bhrigus will come to you in time."
[Yudhishthira] Seeing what result in honouring brahmins, mighty-vowed one, do you honour them? Tell me all this.
[Bhishma] Keshava here, of great mind, will tell you all about the result of honouring brahmins, he who has seen the result, O mighty-vowed ones.
My strength, hearing, speech, mind and eyes and knowledge are not clear today; I think the casting off of my body is not far, and the sun is not moving very fast.
The great dharmas told in the Purana for brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas, and those who follow the ancient rod, learn the rest from Krishna, Partha.
For I know him in truth, Krishna, and what his ancient strength is; Keshava of immeasurable soul, chief of the Kurus, he will tell dharma in doubts.

Krishna created the earth, the sky and heaven; this is the Boar of terrible might, ancient. Below him, the atmosphere, heaven, the four directions and four intermediate directions: this creation too issued forth; he made this ancient universe.
From his navel the lotus arose, in which the immeasurably radiant one himself was born; by him that dreadful darkness was cut, Partha, which stood in the roaring ocean.
In the Krita age dharma was complete; in the Treta age knowledge came; in the Dvapara age, Partha, strength; and in the Kali, Krishna, unrighteousness came to the earth.

Having abandoned what should be abandoned for the destruction of asuras, the cause of what is to be done and not to be done, Partha, what he did and will do and is doing, the god; know this Soma and Shakra too.
He is the maker of all, of all forms, the bearer of all, the maker of all, conqueror of all; the bearer of the trident, the drinker of blood, the terrible; they praise him, known by his deeds.
Gandharvas and apsarases and hundreds of the gods always attend him, and rakshasas wait on him; he alone, wishing to conquer, is the increase of wealth.
At the sacrifice the reciters praise him, the singers of Saman praise him in the Rathantara, brahmins praise him with Brahman-mantras, and the Adhvaryus prepare the oblation for him.
[Marutta] Narada has told me of you as I wandered on the road: that you are my teacher's son; therefore I have supreme joy.
Vidura, the learned, followed him, and the charioteer Sanjaya, and also the great archer Kripa Sharadvata.
Then, seeing his sons, grandsons, brothers and friends lying slain, he said this to me.
Karna entered the Sun, his father, O best of men; Shakuni went to Dvapara, and Dhrishtadyumna to Fire.
